author: Janelle Faignant Arts Correspondent
title: Dark Star Orchestra: 'We play an actual Grateful Dead show' | Rutland Reader | rutlandherald.com
text:
The first time Sandy Troy, a lawyer from San Diego, saw the Grateful Dead live, it was 1969. By 1994 he had been to over 200 Dead shows and written a biography of the band’s founder and legendary lead singer Jerry Garcia.
Drummer Dino English had a similar experience.
“I got on the bus about 1991,” English said, “as they say, ‘got on the bus.’ I didn’t know anything about the Grateful Dead but a friend of mine got tickets to a concert in Kansas City. I was a music major and music fan and had never seen the Grateful Dead. It was a life-changing experience for me. One show, went in and became huge fan. Instantly.”
He was a young musician trying to make a career out of playing in a band, and with the Grateful Dead’s music he found an immediate connection.
“It felt natural, like I didn’t have to try to fit into the music,” English said. “My natural way of playing was conducive to playing this music.”
By 1999, he had auditioned for and joined the Dead tribute band Dark Star Orchestra — and has played more than 3,000 shows since.
“I think I was just ready,” English recalled. “My audition was an actual show. I’d never played with the band, I just got up on stage and played a show with them, and here I am 26 years later.”
The band’s name comes from the song “Dark Star,” an early Dead signature classic written by lyricist Robert Hunter and composed by Jerry Garcia, that evolved from a short song into a 20-minute-plus improvisation on the 1969 album “Live/Dead.” It became a “holy grail” for many fans and exemplifies the essence of a Dark Star Orchestra show.
DSO is comprised of a group of “Deadheads,” known for their authentic recreation of the Grateful Dead shows that kept fans coming back sometimes hundreds of times. The band will be at Rutland’s Paramount Theatre at 7:30 p.m. Thursday, Nov. 13.
Garcia was only 22 when he started the Grateful Dead, which has an estimated 500 songs in its catalog, a mix of blues, country, jazz, folk and psychedelic rock. Beyond learning the songs, Dark Star Orchestra improvises and plays the trademark jams in the same spirit the Dead did.
“Not all of it’s easy,” English said. “Some songs have basic chord changes, but other ones are pretty intricate. There’s a lot of stuff with odd time signatures.”
But DSO does not impersonate the Dead.
“It’s all about the music,” English said. “A few guys have a natural resemblance but it’s not on purpose, it’s just about the music. We play an actual Grateful Dead show. We cover more than the song — we cover an actual full show.”
“We’re playing it arrangement for arrangement, not note for note,” English said. “It would be a disservice to play things note for note in my opinion.”
“The melody, the harmonies, those are all intact; the feel of the tune is intact, but there’s still a huge amount of room for improvisation within the music,” he said. “We’re just basically playing the skeleton of the tune and all the essential elements of the song but there’s plenty of room to play around with it.”
That was at the heart of all the live Dead shows that fans loved and remain loyal to, to this day.
For almost 30 years Dark Star Orchestra has been offering a live Grateful Dead concert experience with a seven-piece band and actual Dead set lists.
“For us it’s a chance to recreate some of the magic that was created for us over the years,” keyboardist and vocalist Rob Barraco states on the website. “We offer a sort of historical perspective at what it might have been like to go to a show in 1985, 1978 or whenever.”
So, if you never had the chance to see a Dead show before, you can now. Chances are, it won’t be your last.
